claim: ARF6 and ARF8 redundantly regulate hypocotyl elongation in Arabidopsis.
source: ARF6 and its closed homolog ARF8 were previously shown to redundantly regulate hypocotyl elongation in Arabidopsis (Nagpal et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nagpal et al., 2005.

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis identified 2037 ARF6-binding sites in the Arabidopsis genome.
source: ChIP-Seq analysis using anti-Myc antibody identified 2037 ARF6-binding sites in the Arabidopsis genome.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental ChIP-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most ARF6 binding sites are in gene promoter regions.
source: Most of the ARF6 binding sites were in the gene promoter regions consistent with its molecular function as a transcription regulator (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data and Figure 1A showing distribution of binding peaks.

claim: The 2037 ARF6 binding sites were linked to 2675 neighbor genes.
source: The 2037 binding sites were linked to 2675 neighbor genes (Figure 1—source data 1A), which were considered ARF6 binding target genes.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: ARF6 binding targets include 40 of the 49 early auxin-induced genes in hypocotyl tissues after 30 min of auxin treatment.
source: The ARF6 binding targets include 40 of the 49 early auxin-induced genes in the hypocotyl tissues after 30 min of auxin treatment (Chapman et al., 2012), but only 1 of the 16 immediate auxin-repressed genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data with published auxin-responsive gene data from Chapman et al., 2012.

claim: ARF6 appears to function mainly as a transcriptional activator.
source: Therefore, ARF6 appears to function mainly as a transcriptional activator, consistent with previous study (Tiwari et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ARF6 binds to auxin-activated genes but not repressed genes, and is supported by citation to Tiwari et al., 2003.

claim: 255 ARF6 binding targets are activated by auxin in hypocotyl tissues.
source: Comparison with auxin-activated genes (Chapman et al., 2012) identified 255 ARF6 binding targets that are activated by auxin in the hypocotyl tissues.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data with published auxin-responsive gene data.

claim: 51% of ARF6 binding targets overlap with BZR1 targets.
source: Interestingly, large portions of ARF6 binding targets overlapped with either targets of BZR1 (51%) or PIF4 (71%) or both (42%) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ChIP-Seq datasets for ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4.

claim: 71% of ARF6 binding targets overlap with PIF4 targets.
source: Interestingly, large portions of ARF6 binding targets overlapped with either targets of BZR1 (51%) or PIF4 (71%) or both (42%) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ChIP-Seq datasets for ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4.

claim: 42% of ARF6 binding targets overlap with both BZR1 and PIF4 targets.
source: Interestingly, large portions of ARF6 binding targets overlapped with either targets of BZR1 (51%) or PIF4 (71%) or both (42%) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ChIP-Seq datasets for ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4.

claim: ARF6 and BZR1 co-occupy the SAUR15 and IAA19 promoters.
source: ChIP-reChIP assays showed that two common targets, SAUR15 and IAA19, were recovered by sequential immunoprecipitation in plants expressing both BZR1-YFP and ARF6-Myc, but not in plants expressing ARF6-Myc only (Figure 1D), indicating that ARF6 and BZR1 co-occupy these promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-reChIP experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: G-box (CACGTG) motifs are highly enriched in ARF6 binding regions associated with auxin-activated genes.
source: Cis-element analysis identified two types of E-box motifs, the G-box (CACGTG), and the Hormone Up at Dawn (HUD, CACATG) motifs (Michael et al., 2008), that are highly enriched in the ARF6 binding regions associated with the auxin-activated genes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on cis-element analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data and is supported by citation to Michael et al., 2008.

claim: HUD (CACATG) motifs are highly enriched in ARF6 binding regions associated with auxin-activated genes.
source: Cis-element analysis identified two types of E-box motifs, the G-box (CACGTG), and the Hormone Up at Dawn (HUD, CACATG) motifs (Michael et al., 2008), that are highly enriched in the ARF6 binding regions associated with the auxin-activated genes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on cis-element analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data and is supported by citation to Michael et al., 2008.

claim: The canonical ARF binding motif AuxRE (TGTCTC) is highly enriched among ARF6 binding regions.
source: The canonical ARF binding motif, AuxRE (TGTCTC), and the binding motif (TGTCGG) recently identified for recombinant ARF1 and ARF5 were also highly enriched among the ARF6 binding regions (Figure 1E; Ulmasov et al., 1999; Boer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cis-element analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data and is supported by citations.

claim: The binding motif TGTCGG is highly enriched among ARF6 binding regions.
source: The canonical ARF binding motif, AuxRE (TGTCTC), and the binding motif (TGTCGG) recently identified for recombinant ARF1 and ARF5 were also highly enriched among the ARF6 binding regions (Figure 1E; Ulmasov et al., 1999; Boer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cis-element analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data and is supported by citations.

claim: About half of the auxin-activated ARF6 binding regions have both core AuxRE (TGTC) and E-box motifs within ±100 base pairs around the binding site.
source: About half of the auxin-activated ARF6 binding regions had both core AuxRE (TGTC) and the E-box motifs within the ±100 base pairs around the binding site, which is much higher than random expectation (only 9%) (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cis-element distribution in ARF6 ChIP-Seq data.

claim: E-box motifs tend to be located close to the core AuxRE, mostly within 20 base pairs.
source: The E-box motifs tend to be located close to the core AuxRE, mostly within 20 base pairs (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of distance distribution between motifs in ARF6 ChIP-Seq data.

claim: ARF6 binding regions having both AuxRE and E-box motifs are significantly more frequently associated with auxin-activated genes than binding regions having only AuxRE.
source: Furthermore, the ARF6 binding regions having both AuxRE and E-box motifs were significantly more frequently associated with auxin-activated genes than binding regions having only AuxRE (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data and auxin-responsive gene data.

claim: ARF6 directly interacts with BZR1 through the C-terminal domain of BZR1.
source: Indeed, ARF6 directly interacted with both BZR1 and PIF4 through the C-terminal domain of BZR1 and the bHLH domain of PIF4 in the yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figures 2A-D.

claim: ARF6 directly interacts with PIF4 through the bHLH domain of PIF4.
source: Indeed, ARF6 directly interacted with both BZR1 and PIF4 through the C-terminal domain of BZR1 and the bHLH domain of PIF4 in the yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figures 2A-D.

claim: Both the middle and C-terminal domains of ARF6 are required for interactions with BZR1 and PIF4.
source: Both the middle and C-terminal domains of ARF6 were required for the interactions with BZR1 and PIF4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data with ARF6 domain deletions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARF6 interacts with BZR1 and PIF4 in vivo.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed that ARF6 interacts with BZR1 and PIF4 in vivo (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BZR1–PIF4 interaction enhances PIF4 interaction with ARF6.
source: In addition, the ARF6–PIF4 interaction was increased by co-transfection with a gain-of-function bzr1-1D protein that is constitutively active irrespective of BR signaling (Wang et al., 2002; Figure 2F), suggesting that BZR1–PIF4 interaction enhances PIF4 interaction with ARF6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F and is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2002.

claim: BZR1 and PIF4 specifically interact with ARF8, but not ARF1 and ARF7.
source: We next examined if BZR1 and PIF4 interact with other ARFs using yeast two-hybrid assays, and the results show that both BZR1 and PIF4 specifically interacted with ARF8, but not ARF1 and ARF7 (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that BZR1 and PIF4 mediate only subsets of auxin responses such as hypocotyl elongation by interacting with specific ARFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figures 2G, 2H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: BZR1 and PIF4 mediate only subsets of auxin responses such as hypocotyl elongation by interacting with specific ARFs.
source: We next examined if BZR1 and PIF4 interact with other ARFs using yeast two-hybrid assays, and the results show that both BZR1 and PIF4 specifically interacted with ARF8, but not ARF1 and ARF7 (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that BZR1 and PIF4 mediate only subsets of auxin responses such as hypocotyl elongation by interacting with specific ARFs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the specificity of BZR1 and PIF4 interactions with ARF6/ARF8 but not other ARFs.

claim: bzr1-1D enhances ARF6 DNA-binding to common target promoters.
source: The ARF6 binding to the promoters of common target genes were increased by BR treatment, as observed for ARF5 on the promoter of SAUR15 (Walcher and Nemhauser, 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 3). In addition, bzr1-1D and PIF4-OX enhanced ARF6 binding to the common targets (SAUR15, SAUR19 and At1g29500), but not to the targets of ARF6 only (At4g12110 and At2g40880), indicating that BZR1 and PIF4 enhance ARF6 DNA-binding in vivo (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2I and citation to Walcher and Nemhauser, 2012.

claim: PIF4-OX enhances ARF6 DNA-binding to common target promoters.
source: In addition, bzr1-1D and PIF4-OX enhanced ARF6 binding to the common targets (SAUR15, SAUR19 and At1g29500), but not to the targets of ARF6 only (At4g12110 and At2g40880), indicating that BZR1 and PIF4 enhance ARF6 DNA-binding in vivo (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ARF6 occupancy is higher at binding regions containing both E-box motifs and AuxRE than regions containing only AuxRE.
source: Based on the signal intensity of ARF6 ChIP-Seq data, ARF6 occupancy is higher at binding regions containing both E-box motifs and AuxRE than regions containing only AuxRE (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ARF6 ChIP-Seq signal intensity shown in Figure 2K.

claim: 2664 genes respond to BR in wild-type plants.
source: We identified 2664 genes that responded to BR in wild-type plants and 4725 genes differentially expressed in the iaa3 mutant compared to wild type (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 4725 genes are differentially expressed in the iaa3 mutant compared to wild type.
source: We identified 2664 genes that responded to BR in wild-type plants and 4725 genes differentially expressed in the iaa3 mutant compared to wild type (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression levels of 1465 BR-regulated genes (55%) are also affected by iaa3, mostly in opposite ways (correlation coefficient = −0.6).
source: Expression levels of many BR-regulated genes (1465, 55%) were also affected by iaa3, and mostly in opposite ways (correlation coefficient = −0.6) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 976 genes co-regulated by BZR1 and PIFs are affected by iaa3.
source: Of 2482 BZR1- and PIFs-co-regulated genes (Oh et al., 2012), 976 genes were affected by iaa3 (350 expected randomly) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of RNA-Seq datasets and is supported by citation to Oh et al., 2012.

claim: Most of the co-regulated genes (70%) are similarly regulated by BZR1 and PIFs, but oppositely affected by iaa3.
source: Heat-map in Figure 3D shows that most of the co-regulated genes (70%) are similarly regulated by BZR1 and PIFs, but oppositely affected by iaa3.
evidence: The claim is based on heat map analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Of the 1616 BR-activated genes detected in wild-type plants, only 276 genes (17.1%) were activated by BR treatment in iaa3.
source: Of the 1616 BR-activated genes detected in wild-type plants, only 276 genes (17.1%) were activated by BR treatment in iaa3, whereas a bigger portion of BR-repressed genes (30% of 1048) were still repressed by BR treatment in iaa3 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 30% of BR-repressed genes were still repressed by BR treatment in iaa3.
source: Of the 1616 BR-activated genes detected in wild-type plants, only 276 genes (17.1%) were activated by BR treatment in iaa3, whereas a bigger portion of BR-repressed genes (30% of 1048) were still repressed by BR treatment in iaa3 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Activation of BR- and auxin-induced genes by bzr1-1D is abolished or diminished by iaa3.
source: Activation of the BR- and auxin-induced genes by bzr1-1D was abolished or diminished by iaa3, but the repression of BR-repressed DWF4 expression was unaffected by iaa3 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The repression of BR-repressed DWF4 expression is unaffected by iaa3.
source: Activation of the BR- and auxin-induced genes by bzr1-1D was abolished or diminished by iaa3, but the repression of BR-repressed DWF4 expression was unaffected by iaa3 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The phosphorylation or accumulation status of BZR1 is not affected in the iaa3 mutant.
source: Consistent with iaa3 mutation not affecting the BZR1 function in repression of gene expression, the phosphorylation or accumulation status of BZR1 was not affected in the iaa3 mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: BR-activated genes are less activated in arf6;arf8 than in wild type.
source: Indeed, BR-activated genes were less activated in arf6;arf8 than in wild type, but BR-repressed genes were normally repressed in arf6;arf8 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: BR-repressed genes are normally repressed in arf6;arf8.
source: Indeed, BR-activated genes were less activated in arf6;arf8 than in wild type, but BR-repressed genes were normally repressed in arf6;arf8 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: BR activation of genes for hypocotyl elongation is dependent on auxin activation of ARFs.
source: These results indicate that BR activation of genes for hypocotyl elongation is dependent on auxin activation of ARFs, whereas BR feedback repression of BR biosynthesis genes is independent of auxin signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BR-activated genes require ARF activity but BR-repressed genes do not.

claim: BR feedback repression of BR biosynthesis genes is independent of auxin signaling.
source: These results indicate that BR activation of genes for hypocotyl elongation is dependent on auxin activation of ARFs, whereas BR feedback repression of BR biosynthesis genes is independent of auxin signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BR-repressed genes are normally repressed in iaa3 and arf6;arf8 mutants.

claim: Auxin-activated genes are less activated by auxin in bri1-116 than in wild type.
source: Auxin-activated genes SAUR15, SAUR19, ACS5, and At4g13790 were less activated by auxin in bri1-116 than in wild type, but bzr1-1D enhanced the auxin activation of these genes in the bri1-116 background (Figure 3I), indicating that BR promotes auxin responsive genes by activating BZR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: bzr1-1D enhances auxin activation of genes in the bri1-116 background.
source: Auxin-activated genes SAUR15, SAUR19, ACS5, and At4g13790 were less activated by auxin in bri1-116 than in wild type, but bzr1-1D enhanced the auxin activation of these genes in the bri1-116 background (Figure 3I), indicating that BR promotes auxin responsive genes by activating BZR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: BR promotes auxin responsive genes by activating BZR1.
source: Auxin-activated genes SAUR15, SAUR19, ACS5, and At4g13790 were less activated by auxin in bri1-116 than in wild type, but bzr1-1D enhanced the auxin activation of these genes in the bri1-116 background (Figure 3I), indicating that BR promotes auxin responsive genes by activating BZR1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that bzr1-1D rescues auxin response in bri1-116.

claim: Auxin activation of genes is reduced in the pif-quadruple mutant (pifq).
source: The auxin activation of these genes was reduced in the pif-quadruple mutant (pifq) lacking four PIFs (PIF1/PIL5, PIF3, PIF4 and PIF5/PIL6) (Shin et al., 2009) and completely abolished by overexpression of PAR1 (PAR1-OX), which inhibits PIF activities (Hao et al., 2012; Figure 3I), consistent with previous observation (Roig-Villanova et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I and citations to Shin et al., 2009 and Hao et al., 2012.

claim: Auxin activation of genes is completely abolished by overexpression of PAR1 (PAR1-OX).
source: The auxin activation of these genes was reduced in the pif-quadruple mutant (pifq) lacking four PIFs (PIF1/PIL5, PIF3, PIF4 and PIF5/PIL6) (Shin et al., 2009) and completely abolished by overexpression of PAR1 (PAR1-OX), which inhibits PIF activities (Hao et al., 2012; Figure 3I), consistent with previous observation (Roig-Villanova et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I and citations to Hao et al., 2012 and Roig-Villanova et al., 2007.

claim: Hypocotyl elongation of the BR receptor mutant bri1 shows diminished response to auxin.
source: Hypocotyl elongation of the BR receptor mutant bri1 shows diminished response to auxin (Figure 4A), as observed previously (Nemhauser et al., 2004), but the auxin-insensitive phenotype of bri1 was fully rescued by bzr1-1D (Figure 4A), indicating that BZR1 mediates BR enhancement of auxin response.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Nemhauser et al., 2004.

claim: The auxin-insensitive phenotype of bri1 is fully rescued by bzr1-1D.
source: Hypocotyl elongation of the BR receptor mutant bri1 shows diminished response to auxin (Figure 4A), as observed previously (Nemhauser et al., 2004), but the auxin-insensitive phenotype of bri1 was fully rescued by bzr1-1D (Figure 4A), indicating that BZR1 mediates BR enhancement of auxin response.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BZR1 mediates BR enhancement of auxin response.
source: Hypocotyl elongation of the BR receptor mutant bri1 shows diminished response to auxin (Figure 4A), as observed previously (Nemhauser et al., 2004), but the auxin-insensitive phenotype of bri1 was fully rescued by bzr1-1D (Figure 4A), indicating that BZR1 mediates BR enhancement of auxin response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that bzr1-1D rescues auxin insensitivity of bri1.

claim: The hypersensitivity of bzr1-1D to auxin is abolished by the iaa3 mutation.
source: The hypersensitivity of bzr1-1D to auxin was abolished by the iaa3 mutation (Figure 4B), suggesting that ARF activity is required for BZR1 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ARF activity is required for BZR1 function.
source: The hypersensitivity of bzr1-1D to auxin was abolished by the iaa3 mutation (Figure 4B), suggesting that ARF activity is required for BZR1 function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that iaa3 abolishes bzr1-1D hypersensitivity to auxin.

claim: Both iaa3 and arf6;arf8 are less sensitive to BR than wild type.
source: Consistently, both iaa3 and arf6;arf8 were less sensitive to BR than was wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ARF6/8 are required for BZR1 promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
source: Furthermore, the bzr1-1D;arf6;arf8 triple mutant and bzr1-1D;iaa3 double mutant showed shorter hypocotyls on the medium containing BR biosynthesis inhibitor BRZ than the bzr1-1D single mutant (Figure 4D,E), indicating that ARF6/8 are required for BZR1 promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: pifq is less sensitive to auxin than wild type.
source: Finally, to determine whether PIFs are required for auxin response, we checked the hypocotyl response to auxin in pifq and PAR1-OX. Compared with wild type, pifq was less sensitive and PAR1-OX was almost insensitive to auxin (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PAR1-OX is almost insensitive to auxin.
source: Finally, to determine whether PIFs are required for auxin response, we checked the hypocotyl response to auxin in pifq and PAR1-OX. Compared with wild type, pifq was less sensitive and PAR1-OX was almost insensitive to auxin (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ARF, BZR1 and PIFs are interdependent in promoting hypocotyl elongation.
source: These results indicate that ARF, BZR1 and PIFs are interdependent in promoting hypocotyl elongation, consistent with their cooperative regulation of a core set of genes involved in hypocotyl cell elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing mutual dependence of these factors.

claim: PAR1 interacts with BEE2 and HBI1.
source: The Arabidopsis Interactome map showed that PAR1 interacts with another bHLH transcription factor BEE2 (Arabidopsis Interactome Mapping Consortium, 2011), which was shown to be involved in BR regulation of cell elongation (Friedrichsen et al., 2002). Our yeast two-hybrid assays confirmed that PAR1 interacts with BEE2 and its close homolog HBI1 as well (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Arabidopsis Interactome Mapping Consortium, 2011 and Friedrichsen et al., 2002.

claim: BEE2 and HBI1 interact with ARF6.
source: Like PIF4, BEE2, and HBI1 also interact with ARF6 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Transgenic plants overexpressing HBI1-SRDX are less sensitive to auxin than wild type.
source: Transgenic plants overexpressing a dominant repressor version of HBI1 (HBI1-SRDX) (Bai et al., 2012a) were less sensitive to auxin than was wild type (Figure 5C), supporting a positive role of HBI1 in auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 5C and citation to Bai et al., 2012a.

claim: HBI1 has a positive role in auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
source: Transgenic plants overexpressing a dominant repressor version of HBI1 (HBI1-SRDX) (Bai et al., 2012a) were less sensitive to auxin than was wild type (Figure 5C), supporting a positive role of HBI1 in auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HBI1-SRDX reduces auxin sensitivity.

claim: ARF6 interacts with multiple bHLH transcription factors as co-transcriptional regulators.
source: These results suggest that ARF6 interacts with multiple bHLH transcription factors as co-transcriptional regulators, and PAR1 attenuates auxin response through direct inactivation of these bHLH transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ARF6 interacts with PIF4, BEE2, and HBI1.

claim: PAR1 attenuates auxin response through direct inactivation of bHLH transcription factors.
source: These results suggest that ARF6 interacts with multiple bHLH transcription factors as co-transcriptional regulators, and PAR1 attenuates auxin response through direct inactivation of these bHLH transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PAR1 interacts with bHLH factors and PAR1-OX reduces auxin sensitivity.

claim: pre-amiR and IBH1-OX plants are less sensitive to auxin than wild type.
source: Indeed, knock down of multiple PREs (PRE1, PRE2, PRE5 and PRE6) by artificial micro-RNA (pre-amiR) or overexpression of IBH1 (IBH1-OX) (Bai et al., 2012a, 2012b), significantly reduced the sensitivity of transgenic plants to auxin in terms of both hypocotyl elongation and gene expression (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation and gene expression data shown in Figures 5C and 5D, and citations to Bai et al., 2012a, 2012b.

claim: PRE1 expression is high in young and growing tissues.
source: The expression levels of IBH1 and PRE1 are developmentally regulated; PRE1 expression is high in young and growing tissues, whereas IBH1 expression is high in mature and growth-arrested tissues (Zhang et al., 2009; Ikeda et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2009 and Ikeda et al., 2012.

claim: IBH1 expression is high in mature and growth-arrested tissues.
source: The expression levels of IBH1 and PRE1 are developmentally regulated; PRE1 expression is high in young and growing tissues, whereas IBH1 expression is high in mature and growth-arrested tissues (Zhang et al., 2009; Ikeda et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2009 and Ikeda et al., 2012.

claim: Auxin treatment induces bigger fold changes of PREs and SAUR15 expression levels in young stems than in mature stems.
source: We confirmed the developmental regulation of expression of PRE1, PRE5 and IBH1 (Figure 5E), and found that auxin treatment induced bigger fold changes of the PREs and SAUR15 expression levels in young stems than in mature stems (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The reduced auxin sensitivity of SAUR15 gene in mature stem is restored in PRE1-OX, HBI1-OX and PIF4-OX plants.
source: The reduced auxin sensitivity of the SAUR15 gene in the mature stem was restored in the PRE1-OX, HBI1-OX and PIF4-OX plants (Figure 5F), supporting that developmental regulation of PREs and IBH1 impacts auxin sensitivity through PIF4 and HBI1.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Developmental regulation of PREs and IBH1 impacts auxin sensitivity through PIF4 and HBI1.
source: The reduced auxin sensitivity of the SAUR15 gene in the mature stem was restored in the PRE1-OX, HBI1-OX and PIF4-OX plants (Figure 5F), supporting that developmental regulation of PREs and IBH1 impacts auxin sensitivity through PIF4 and HBI1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that overexpression of PRE1, HBI1, or PIF4 restores auxin sensitivity in mature stems.

claim: DWF4 expression is high in young stems but low in mature stems.
source: The expression level of BR biosynthesis gene DWF4 was high in young stems but low in mature stems (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: BZR1 is less phosphorylated in young stems than in mature stems.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern of DWF4, BZR1 was less phosphorylated in the young stems than in the mature stems (Figure 5H), indicating that BZR1 is more activated in the young tissues (He et al., 2002; Gampala et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: BZR1 is more activated in young tissues.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern of DWF4, BZR1 was less phosphorylated in the young stems than in the mature stems (Figure 5H), indicating that BZR1 is more activated in the young tissues (He et al., 2002; Gampala et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BZR1 is less phosphorylated in young stems, and is supported by citations to He et al., 2002; Gampala et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2007.

claim: Activation of BZR1 by bzr1-1D mutation increases auxin sensitivity of SAUR15 expression in mature stem.
source: Indeed, activation of BZR1 by the bzr1-1D mutation increased auxin sensitivity of SAUR15 expression in the mature stem (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Developmental regulation of BZR1 and HLH factors contributes to changes of auxin sensitivity over the progression of organ development.
source: Together, these results suggest that developmental regulation of BZR1 and HLH factors contributes to the changes of auxin sensitivity over the progression of organ development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that BZR1 activity and HLH factor expression are developmentally regulated and affect auxin sensitivity.

claim: GA-activated genes are enriched in the common targets of ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4.
source: A comparison of ARF6 targets with BZR1 and PIF4 targets revealed that GA-activated genes are enriched in the common targets of ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4 (Figure 1I), suggesting that ARF6 is also involved in GA response.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ChIP-Seq datasets shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ARF6 is involved in GA response.
source: A comparison of ARF6 targets with BZR1 and PIF4 targets revealed that GA-activated genes are enriched in the common targets of ARF6, BZR1, and PIF4 (Figure 1I), suggesting that ARF6 is also involved in GA response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enrichment of GA-activated genes among ARF6 targets.

claim: RGA interacts with the middle domain and, to a lesser extent, the DNA binding domain of ARF6.
source: In yeast two-hybrid assays, RGA interacted with the middle domain and, to a lesser extent, the DNA binding domain of ARF6 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: RGA interacts with activator ARFs (ARF6, ARF7 and ARF8), but not repressor ARF1.
source: RGA also interacted with other activator ARFs (ARF6, ARF7 and ARF8), but not repressor ARF1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RGA directly interacts with ARF6 in vitro.
source: In addition, HA-RGA, but not HA-YFP, was pulled down by ARF6-Myc in vitro (Figure 6B), and RGA-GFP was co-immunoprecipitated with ARF6-Myc in Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RGA directly interacts with ARF6 in vivo.
source: In addition, HA-RGA, but not HA-YFP, was pulled down by ARF6-Myc in vitro (Figure 6B), and RGA-GFP was co-immunoprecipitated with ARF6-Myc in Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 6C). These results demonstrate that RGA directly interacts with ARF6.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RGA competes with PIF4/BZR1 for interaction with ARF6.
source: Since the middle domain of ARF6 also mediates the ARF6-PIF4/BZR1 interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it is likely that RGA competes with PIF4/BZR1 for interaction with ARF6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RGA and PIF4/BZR1 interact with the same domain of ARF6.

claim: RGA disrupts the ARF6–PIF4 interaction.
source: Indeed, the ARF6-PIF4 interaction was reduced by rga-Δ17, which is a stable form of RGA due to deletion of the N-terminal DELLA domain (Bai et al., 2012b; Figure 6D), suggesting that RGA disrupts the ARF6–PIF4 interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D and citation to Bai et al., 2012b.

claim: RGA inhibits ARF6 binding to the IAA19 promoter in DNA pull-down assay.
source: Biotin-labeled IAA19 promoter fragment containing AuxRE effectively pulled down MBP-ARF6 in the absence of RGA, but not after pre-incubation of MBP-ARF6 with GST-RGA (Figure 6E), indicating that RGA prevents ARF6 from binding to target DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: RGA prevents ARF6 from binding to target DNA.
source: Biotin-labeled IAA19 promoter fragment containing AuxRE effectively pulled down MBP-ARF6 in the absence of RGA, but not after pre-incubation of MBP-ARF6 with GST-RGA (Figure 6E), indicating that RGA prevents ARF6 from binding to target DNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the DNA pull-down assay results.

claim: RGA inhibits ARF6 binding to target genes in vivo.
source: ChIP assay confirmed that RGA inhibits ARF6 binding to target genes in vivo (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ARF6 increases IAA19 promoter activity.
source: Transient reporter gene expression assays showed that ARF6 increases IAA19 promoter activity, but the ARF6 effect was abolished by co-transfection with RGA (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by transient reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The ARF6 effect on IAA19 promoter activity is abolished by co-transfection with RGA.
source: Transient reporter gene expression assays showed that ARF6 increases IAA19 promoter activity, but the ARF6 effect was abolished by co-transfection with RGA (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by transient reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: DELLA interacts with ARF6 and inhibits ARF6 DNA-binding to modulate ARF6 target gene expression.
source: These data demonstrate that DELLA interacts with ARF6 and inhibits ARF6 DNA-binding to modulate ARF6 target gene expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of interaction assays, DNA-binding assays, and reporter assays.

claim: GA promotes cell elongation by enhancing auxin/ARF-mediated responses.
source: The DELLA inhibition of ARF6 suggests that GA promotes cell elongation by enhancing auxin/ARF-mediated responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DELLA inhibits ARF6 activity.

claim: The GA-promotion of hypocotyl elongation is much reduced in iaa3 and arf6;arf8 mutants compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, the GA-promotion of hypocotyl elongation was much reduced in the iaa3 and arf6;arf8 mutants compared to the wild type (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that auxin activation of ARFs is necessary for the GA promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Auxin activation of ARFs is necessary for GA promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
source: Indeed, the GA-promotion of hypocotyl elongation was much reduced in the iaa3 and arf6;arf8 mutants compared to the wild type (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that auxin activation of ARFs is necessary for the GA promotion of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that iaa3 and arf6;arf8 mutants show reduced GA response.

claim: Auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation is compromised in the GA-insensitive mutant gai-1.
source: In addition, the auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation was compromised in the GA-insensitive mutant gai-1 (Peng et al., 1997) and in wild-type plants grown on the medium containing GA biosynthesis inhibitor paclobutrazol (PAC) (Figure 6I), both of which accumulate DELLA proteins, but was nearly normal in the PAC-treated della pentuple mutant (della) lacking all five members of the DELLA family (Wang et al., 2009; Figure 6I), indicating that accumulation of DELLA proteins inhibits auxin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 6I and citation to Peng et al., 1997.

claim: Auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation is compromised in wild-type plants grown on medium containing paclobutrazol (PAC).
source: In addition, the auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation was compromised in the GA-insensitive mutant gai-1 (Peng et al., 1997) and in wild-type plants grown on the medium containing GA biosynthesis inhibitor paclobutrazol (PAC) (Figure 6I), both of which accumulate DELLA proteins, but was nearly normal in the PAC-treated della pentuple mutant (della) lacking all five members of the DELLA family (Wang et al., 2009; Figure 6I), indicating that accumulation of DELLA proteins inhibits auxin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation is nearly normal in PAC-treated della pentuple mutant.
source: In addition, the auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation was compromised in the GA-insensitive mutant gai-1 (Peng et al., 1997) and in wild-type plants grown on the medium containing GA biosynthesis inhibitor paclobutrazol (PAC) (Figure 6I), both of which accumulate DELLA proteins, but was nearly normal in the PAC-treated della pentuple mutant (della) lacking all five members of the DELLA family (Wang et al., 2009; Figure 6I), indicating that accumulation of DELLA proteins inhibits auxin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl elongation data shown in Figure 6I and citation to Wang et al., 2009.

claim: Accumulation of DELLA proteins inhibits auxin sensitivity.
source: In addition, the auxin promotion of hypocotyl elongation was compromised in the GA-insensitive mutant gai-1 (Peng et al., 1997) and in wild-type plants grown on the medium containing GA biosynthesis inhibitor paclobutrazol (PAC) (Figure 6I), both of which accumulate DELLA proteins, but was nearly normal in the PAC-treated della pentuple mutant (della) lacking all five members of the DELLA family (Wang et al., 2009; Figure 6I), indicating that accumulation of DELLA proteins inhibits auxin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that conditions accumulating DELLA reduce auxin sensitivity, while della mutant restores it.

claim: GA-induced degradation of DELLAs allows ARF6, together with BZR1 and PIF4, to bind to target DNA and activate gene expression and hypocotyl cell elongation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the GA-induced degradation of DELLAs allows ARF6, together with BZR1 and PIF4, to bind to target DNA and to activate gene expression and hypocotyl cell elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing DELLA inhibits ARF6 DNA-binding and auxin/GA responses require ARF6.

claim: Hypocotyl cell elongation is controlled by major hormonal and environmental pathways through a central circuit of interacting transcription regulators.
source: Our study demonstrates that hypocotyl cell elongation is controlled by major hormonal and environmental pathways through a central circuit of interacting transcription regulators.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The auxin and BR pathways mainly converge through BZR–ARF interaction at shared target promoters.
source: Consistent with our genetic data and previous analysis of BR-auxin co-regulation of the SAUR15 promoter (Walcher and Nemhauser, 2012), our genomic and biochemical experiments showed direct interaction between BZR1 and ARF6 at the promoters of a large set of genomic targets, demonstrating that the auxin and BR pathways mainly converge through BZR–ARF interaction at shared target promoters.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genomic and biochemical data showing BZR1-ARF6 interactions at target promoters, and is supported by citation to Walcher and Nemhauser, 2012.

claim: Light signaling mediated by phytochromes induces degradation of PIFs.
source: Light signaling mediated by phytochromes induces degradation of PIFs (Leivar and Quail, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leivar and Quail, 2011.

claim: ARF6 shares most of its binding target genes with PIF4.
source: In this study, we show that ARF6 shares most of its binding target genes with PIF4 and they interdependently activate shared target promoters, which explains the requirement of PIFs for auxin responsive gene expression and hypocotyl elongation and the requirement of auxin for skotomorphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ChIP-Seq datasets showing 71% overlap between ARF6 and PIF4 targets.

claim: ARF6 and PIF4 interdependently activate shared target promoters.
source: In this study, we show that ARF6 shares most of its binding target genes with PIF4 and they interdependently activate shared target promoters, which explains the requirement of PIFs for auxin responsive gene expression and hypocotyl elongation and the requirement of auxin for skotomorphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and biochemical data showing mutual dependence of ARF6 and PIF4.

claim: PIFs are required for auxin responsive gene expression and hypocotyl elongation.
source: In this study, we show that ARF6 shares most of its binding target genes with PIF4 and they interdependently activate shared target promoters, which explains the requirement of PIFs for auxin responsive gene expression and hypocotyl elongation and the requirement of auxin for skotomorphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic data showing pifq and PAR1-OX reduce auxin responses.

claim: Auxin is required for skotomorphogenesis.
source: In this study, we show that ARF6 shares most of its binding target genes with PIF4 and they interdependently activate shared target promoters, which explains the requirement of PIFs for auxin responsive gene expression and hypocotyl elongation and the requirement of auxin for skotomorphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the interdependence of ARF6 and PIF4 in regulating hypocotyl elongation.

claim: PIFs are considered a central hub for integrating environmental and developmental signals.
source: PIFs are considered a central hub for integrating environmental and developmental signals (Leivar and Quail, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leivar and Quail, 2011.

claim: Temperature and circadian clock transcriptionally regulate members of PIF family.
source: In addition to light, temperature and the circadian clock transcriptionally regulate members of PIF family (Nozue et al., 2007; Koini et al., 2009), and consequently alter auxin synthesis as well as auxin sensitivity through the BAP module.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nozue et al., 2007 and Koini et al., 2009.

claim: Temperature and circadian clock alter auxin synthesis and auxin sensitivity through the BAP module.
source: In addition to light, temperature and the circadian clock transcriptionally regulate members of PIF family (Nozue et al., 2007; Koini et al., 2009), and consequently alter auxin synthesis as well as auxin sensitivity through the BAP module.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the regulation of PIFs by temperature and circadian clock, and the role of PIFs in the BAP module.

claim: GA, BR, auxin, and PIF4 increase the transcription levels of several PRE members.
source: Considering that GA, BR, auxin, and PIF4 increase the transcription levels of several PRE members (Chapman et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2012b), the HLH/bHLH modules appear to form positive feedback loops, which potentially re-enforce the activation of the BAP module and help maintain the growing condition in the dark or in young developing organs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2012b.

claim: The HLH/bHLH modules form positive feedback loops that re-enforce activation of the BAP module.
source: Considering that GA, BR, auxin, and PIF4 increase the transcription levels of several PRE members (Chapman et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2012b), the HLH/bHLH modules appear to form positive feedback loops, which potentially re-enforce the activation of the BAP module and help maintain the growing condition in the dark or in young developing organs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BAP components activate PRE expression, and PREs enhance BAP activity.

claim: Decrease of HBI1 expression mediates growth arrest and defense activation in response to pathogen infection.
source: The increase of IBH1 expression appears to mediate, at least partly, inactivation of hormone responses in mature organs (Figure 5), whereas a decrease of HBI1 expression mediates growth arrest and defense activation in response to pathogen infection (Fan et al., 2014; Malinovsky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fan et al., 2014 and Malinovsky et al., 2014.

claim: GA has been shown to promote hypocotyl elongation by removing DELLA repression of BZR1 and PIF4.
source: GA has been shown to promote hypocotyl elongation by removing DELLA repression of BZR1 and PIF4.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: DELLA inhibits both protein–DNA and protein–protein interactions of the BAP module.
source: Similar to DELLA inhibition of BZR1 and PIFs, DELLA also inhibits DNA-binding of ARF6. In contrast to the cooperative interactions among BZR1, ARF6, and PIF4, the DELLA protein RGA inhibits ARF6–PIF4 interaction. As such, DELLA inhibits both protein–DNA and protein–protein interactions of the BAP module, providing presumably coordinated and coherent control of all three components of the BAP module.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that DELLA inhibits ARF6 DNA-binding and disrupts ARF6-PIF4 interaction.

claim: The major growth-regulation pathways (auxin, BR, GA, and phytochrome) converge at the BAP/D module to control hypocotyl cell elongation.
source: Together, our study illustrates that the major growth-regulation pathways, auxin, BR, GA, and phytochrome, converge at the BAP/D module to control hypocotyl cell elongation (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the study and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The BAP/D module coupled with the HLH/bHLH module forms the central growth regulation network that integrates hormonal, environmental, and developmental inputs into decisions about hypocotyl cell elongation.
source: We propose that the BAP/D module coupled with the HLH/bHLH module forms the central growth regulation network that integrates hormonal, environmental, and developmental inputs into the decisions about hypocotyl cell elongation (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 7.
